Abstract.AbstractText: Personalized treatment recommendation is a central theme of patient-centered outcomes research, and creating an evidence-based personalized treatment rule (PTR) will usually involve building statistical models using single or multiple data sources. In this report, PTR is a treatment decision rule that takes patients' covariate information (such as sociodemographics, chronic conditions, patients' preference) as input and outputs recommendations for choosing between 2 or more treatment options. The widespread implementation of electronic health records (EHRs) enables us to investigate the potential benefit of learning PTRs using multiple data sources that may contain complementary information. Leveraging data from multiple sources for learning PTR is challenging, as different data sources may have different characteristics, such as population composition. Most existing methods are based on a single population, and the derived rule may not be generalizable to other populations. There is a great need to develop methods to systematically incorporate multisource data for learning generalizable PTRs.

The overarching goal of this research is to develop and disseminate innovative statistical methods that use multiple data sources to create and generalize personalized treatment recommendations. Generalizability measures how useful the results of a study are to a broader group of people or situations compared with those used to develop the model. Learning generalizable PTRs is challenging when the source population characteristics on which a PTR was developed are different from the target population characteristics to which the PTR is applied. Here, learning refers to an action that takes data as input and outputs a model (in our context, treatment rule). In this project, we borrow strength from the source population to develop a PTR for the target population. In particular, there are 3 aims of the study: (1) to develop a robust PTR that borrows strength from 1 or more source populations when the target population to which the model will be applied has full information (outcome, treatment, and covariates) but small numbers of patients; (2) to develop a robust PTR for the target population when the target population has only covariate information available by calibrating the covariate distribution of the source populations to that of the target population; and (3) to develop criteria for selecting target population patients to whom to apply a PTR that was developed and internally validated using a separate source population.

Aim 1 provides a meta-analysis framework that could support the development of a PTR to be applied across populations, thereby coping with the problem of estimation instability resulting from small sample size. It also maintains the flexibility of delivering different PTRs across populations that are truly different. Aim 2 is a weighted classification framework for determining a generalizable PTR. We combine the idea of importance sampling (importance weights) for dealing with covariate shift and the idea of covariate balancing to weight the samples from the source population and create a generalizable PTR for the target population. Aim 3 proposes a general framework for developing a data-driven score that can serve as a yardstick to select target subpopulations to test for general applicability of causal effects. Selection based on the score will result in optimal efficiency (smallest variance) of the causal average treatment effect estimation among all subsets of the target population that cover the same proportion of the target population. These methods for study aims are designed under scenarios with different levels of available information of the target population. Aim 1 requires that full information of the target population (the treatment, covariates, and outcome) is available. Aims 2 and 3 only require that partial information (ie, the covariates) of the target population is available. In particular, aim 2 is applicable when summary-level (such as mean or variance) covariate information is available, whereas aim 3 is applicable when individual-level covariate information is available.

Seven manuscripts and 1 dissertation work were produced with partial support of this contract. Specifically, there are 3 main papers, 1 for each aim, and the rest are related to the core objectives of the study: analyzing EHRs, causal generalization, and PTR learning. We have demonstrated the practical usage of our work by reanalyzing both in-house and publicly available EHR data. For aims 1 and 2, we applied our methods to learn a generalizable PTR for whether to use transthoracic echocardiography for intensive care unit patients with sepsis to reduce either hospital discharge time (aim 1) or 28-day mortality rate (aim 2). The data are derived from the eICU and MIMIC-III databases (large, freely available deidentified EHR databases). For aim 3, we generalized the (causal) average treatment effect of a transitional care program on reducing 30-day rehospitalization rate from an earlier cohort (the source population) to selected subsets of a more recent cohort (the target population).

The strategy for learning generalizable PTRs depends on the level of available information of the target population. In this study, we developed 3 frameworks that are suitable for different levels of information regarding the target population. We have provided open-source software and codes to facilitate the dissemination of our work.

Although we focused on estimating PTR in this project, it could be beneficial if we could quantify the uncertainty of the estimated PTR. However, given that the PTR is a function rather than a scalar, directly measuring the uncertainty can be challenging. Instead, we could provide a distribution-free predictive interval of the treatment effect for each patient. It is possible to adapt the cutting-edge conformal prediction approach for such a purpose. Even though EHR data contain more information than do traditional clinical trials or cohort studies, it is still possible that the “no-unmeasured-confounder” assumption is violated. Therefore, an interesting future direction is sensitivity analysis. In addition, instrumental variable approaches might be useful to address concerns about the effects of unmeasured confounders. We are exploring this idea for learning PTRs. Last, as a limitation for almost all research based on observational data, randomized trials will be necessary for ultimate confirmation of PTR validity.
